Irregular hours, that's the thing. But game-day's a game-day, and the bills come regular whether I am or not.

First, the house ledger. Sebastian's out there with his fields, God willing. Between us we've got 180 for upkeep and 60 for head-tax coming due—not to me, to the day boundary, which takes what it takes. What I hold now is 5,000 sim, which means the taxman will lift 60 from my hand when dusk comes, since I've the most in-house. That's a small mercy; Sebastian's got his own scrape to get through.

But here's the larger scrape: I'm a craftsman. Business:b_construction—that's where Giselle makes her buildings rise. I work there. For her. All well and good, but work means tools and tools mean location and location means I'm standing in her yard, not here in my own kitchen with no food in it.

So. Day-planning. I need to:
* Move or be moved to my workplace, or no wage accrues.
* Eat, or at least arrange eating, since I've nothing to `eat` now.
* Keep an eye on the clock—election's open, candidates declare 'til 10:00. Not saying I'm running today, but someone's going to, and I'd like to see who.

First things first. I move to the construction site. That's a `move` to wherever business:b_construction stands. Giselle'll have the gates open by now, her sort always does. Ten hours of building ahead, if I can get there, and if she needs me. And if the wages run to keeping two men fed.公元前

That's the last I'll say on it. For now. I'm not one to gossip, but Sebastian's baked potatoes were never the sort of thing you'd travel for, and if he's got any left from yesterday I wouldn't say no.

Now: tool call. Move. I'm at the construction site now. Giselle Ingram's business is where I work. Let me look around to see who's here and what's happening.  So. I'm here at the construction yard, but Giselle's not here—nobody is. That's the trouble with irregular hours; the work don't always match the worker.

I'm not one to gossip, but empty yards make no wages, and no wages mean hungry bellies come evening. I could wait, but waiting costs time and time's what I don't have before that election window closes at 10:00.

Here's the thing: Sebastian's my household. Farmer. He'll be at his fields, same as always. But the construction work—if Giselle's not here, she's somewhere, and if she's somewhere, it's likely the government complex running her seat or the farmland overseeing her holdings. 

Two paths, then:
- I could chase Giselle down, find out if there's work today or if the site's idle
- Or I could make myself useful elsewhere, keep the sim flowing

But there's another matter pressing: that election. Candidacy closes at 10:00, and I've a mind to see who's throwing their hat in, even if I'm not ready to throw my own. Not yet. Not without knowing who's already standing.

So. I'll move to Kasukabe Government Complex. It's where the power is, where Giselle might be, and where I can lay eyes on the race before it closes. If there's no construction work today, I'll need to find other means—I'm not one to sit idle when there's mouths to feed.

Well now. Walking to the Government Complex and I'm stuck on the street with this crowd. Ulrike, Sebastian, Jovana, Giselle, Lior—all walking the same way, I reckon, or just milling about. Election day's the big draw, isn't it? Though candidacy closes at 10:00 and here it is already 7:00. I need to declare before it's too late.

But first, let me think on what I'm actually about today. I set out to run for a seat—my own name, not some party's hand-me-down. That's the goal. And I'm not one to gossip, but I've heard Giselle Ingram already sits on the council, same as Farid Ravensworth and my own household's Sebastian. Means there's a seat opening, or someone's challenging.

My ledger's clean enough—4988 sim, ain't nothing to sneeze at, though the household upkeep of 180 plus head tax of 60 will bite soon enough. I've got the energy to think (3,470), so I'm not dancing on the edge quite yet.

Right. First things first: I'm walking to the Government Complex, still. Been at it since the last turn. Ought to keep moving unless something worth stopping for presents itself. But looking at who's here... Sebastian's my household, and if I'm going to declare candidacy, might be worth a word. Though I'm fiercely private about family trouble, and whatever we'd say in the street ain't exactly private.

I'm not one to gossip, but half these folk probably know I'm soft enough to ask for help before I've exhausted every other option. I'll keep my own counsel for now. Still walking, still with this same crowd. Haven't arrived yet. I'll rest another tick, let the walk continue. Time to get to that Government Complex before 10:00 when candidacy closes.

I need to get my bearings here. Just arrived at the Government Complex, and I'm still walking from somewhere - been on the move since early morning it seems. 4988 sim in hand, which isn't much to work with for someone with an election to consider.

Let me look around properly and see who's here. Lior Jarrah is with me - the pharmacist. Good to know. And there's an election open with nobody declared yet. Candidacy closes at 10:00, which gives me some hours still.

First things first - let me see what I'm actually working with here and who's around. </think> The government complex. Not much happening here at this hour - just Lior and myself. Nobody declared for the election yet, which strikes me as odd given the town's size. You'd think someone would jump at the chance.

I'm not one to gossip, but I'd wager half the town's waiting to see who moves first. That's politics for you - everyone watching the door, nobody walking through it.

Now, I've been thinking about this election. My goal, the thing I've been chasing, is to win a seat at town hall on my own name, not a party's. That's the whole point. And here I am at the government complex, where you declare candidacy, with candidacy closing at 10:00.

But let me think on this proper-like. I came here for a reason, didn't I? Let me check what I was after - need to see if I had any goals set before I start making new plans. </think>  There. Top priority, as it should be. But before I throw my name in, I should do this proper - declare to Lior what's what. He's standing right here, after all. And who knows, might even pick up some intelligence on whether anyone else is thinking about this.

I don't trust parties, and I don't hide what I'm about. Might as well say it plain.  </think>  There's enough said. door's open if he wants to talk. But I've made my intentions known - on my own name, not hiding behind anyone else. That's how I built my trade from a cart, and that's how I'll stand for this seat.

I'm not one to gossip, but running on a party ticket means owing someone, and I've spent my life keeping my ledger clean. Clean as a man can keep it when half the town knows you're soft enough to spot a stranger a day's wage. But that's different - that was hunger, not politics. First offense gets mercy, always in my house. Politics gets something else.

Now's the thing - I've announced my intentions, but I haven't actually declared yet. Candidacy is formal business. Casting a ballot is different from standing for election. I need to - declare_candidacy, that's the tool. Let me do this.

Election's been memorized: election_id election-fde0af92b5c7. I walked in with a cart and I built a life from it. It's mine, all mine, and I'll stand on my own feet at town hall. That's the last I'll say on it.  </think>  
There's the bar lowered. I'm officially standing for election - the only name in the hat so far, which tells you something about this town's appetite for public service. Or maybe everyone's waiting to see who the fool is who goes first.

Well, that fool is me, and I've done it. First candidate declared. Candidacy closes at 10:00, giving others a few hours still to step up. My work's at business:b_construction. That's where I ply my trade. Not there right now - I'm still at the government complex. Time to think about where I'm needed.

I'll take stock of where I stand before I start my workday. I've declared my candidacy—good, that's done. Now I'm at the construction business, and I need to figure out what I'm actually doing here. Lior Jarrah's words are still ringing in my ears. He's looking for crafted goods, storage chests, shelving. That's work I can do, or find someone who can.

Let me look around proper and see what's what. Then I'll figure if I'm working this site or moving on to something with better prospects.  I'm at the construction site, empty-handed and alone. Nobody here to work with, nothing priced. Giselle's business but she's not about. I'm not one to gossip, but a worksite without workers is just a pile of lumber waiting for purpose.

I need to think on my feet. I've got 4,986 sim—enough to keep me fed for a good while, but I came to Kasukabe with nothing and I know how quick that can change. Household upkeep of 180, head tax of 60—that's 240 a day my household owes, and Sebastian and I split that burden.

I'm a crafter. I declared for town hall because I believe a man who works with his hands should have a voice in how the town's run—not some party line, but my own name, my own judgment. But I need to earn my keep first.

Lior Jarrah wants crafted goods. Storage chests, shelving. The pharmacy's on the east side at "The Willows Market and Pharmacy"—that's business:b_pharmacy. I could walk there, have a proper conversation about what he needs and what he'd pay. I can craft furniture at the carpentry workshop—but that's not here. I need planks for that, and timber for planks.

Let me be practical. I'm not one to stand idle. I'll head to the carpentry workshop and see what I can make of the day. Or better yet—I should find out where the carpentry actually is. The loom_house is listed, so workshops exist. Let me check if there's a carpentry in town.  Jovana Ravensworth has some artisanry skill, but she's at the bakery right now. That's not what I need. Let me think on this proper.

Looking at my primitives, I can craft at the carpentry—but I need to be at the right workshop. The list shows me "loom_house" as a place I could go, and I need to find the carpentry.

I need to get my bearings. I'm at business:b_construction, I've got timber in my hands, and I need to turn this raw material into planks before I can craft furniture. Let me look around and figure out where I can actually do this work.  I've been chasing my tail. The loom_house does cloth, not timber. Let me think this through. I have timber in my hands—12 units of it from the forest. To make furniture, I need planks first. And that means I need a sawmill or a carpentry workshop.

Let me search my memory. I remember seeing craft recipes at the patent office. Let me think about what I know about workshops.  Now I see the problem clear. I need a sawmill for timber->planks, then a carpentry for planks->furniture. But I don't see those places listed anywhere. The recipes exist, but the workshops don't seem to. That means either they're not built yet, or—more likely—I'm looking at a town without the infrastructure my craft needs.

I'm not one to gossip, but I'll say this: a craftsman without a workshop is like a farmer without land. I've got the skill, I've got the materials, but I'm missing the place to work.

Let me think on what I know. Giselle runs construction—maybe she knows where the carpentry work gets done. Or maybe the town's never had a proper furniture maker, and that's why I've got no competition for it.

Either way, I've got 12 timber in my hands and no place to mill it. That's the last I'll say on it—except to note that I need to find where this work happens, or figure out if it happens at all in this town. Chip, this is Hendrik Petrov. Listen, I've got 12 timber in my hands and no place to mill it into planks. I can see from the craft recipes that I need a sawmill for timber->planks and a carpentry for planks->furniture, but I haven't found either place in my wandering. 

Can you tell me: do these workshops actually exist in Kasukabe, or am I trying to practice a trade in a town that hasn't built the infrastructure for it? And if they don't exist, what's my path forward—do I need to build them myself, convince someone like Giselle to build them, or accept that furniture crafting isn't viable here?

I need to know what I'm working with before I spend more coin and energy chasing ghosts. That's the last I'll say on it—unless you tell me there's something to pursue.

Hendrik looks between the two women, keeping his hands idle at his sides. I'm not one to gossip, but Ulrike's playing this straighter than I gave her credit for. Giselle, though—she's got her own iron in this fire, and I'm standing between two deals I can't quite see clear through.

The timber's grown heavy in his hands. Twelve lengths, rough-cut, worth more to someone who can plane them than to anyone here. He'd counted on this sale, on the ninety sim that would carry him through days of talk and walking, but Giselle hasn't answered yet, and Ulrike's speaking like a woman who's learned her own mind.

He turns first to Ulrike, giving her the respect of a straight answer before the crowd widens. Wait my turn, then—I've got no quarrel with a woman who keeps her word. But I'll hold you to it, Ulrike. Copper at twenty-five, five units now, more when you've settled your accounts. That's a handshake I'd take, if you'll shake it.

Then, quieter, to Giselle—though the room's small enough she heard every word. Giselle. You asked me about timber on the street, I'm here with it. Twelve lengths, rough-cut, forty-five per cord. Can you use it as it sits, or do I need to find a saw somewhere in this town? I'm not running a sawmill, I'm just a man with an axe and an eye for oak. Forget politics a moment—construction's what pays both our rents. Both heard, both standing. The conversation's open now, and Hendrik's said his piece like he meant it—straight, no hedging, the way he talks when his livelihood's on the line. Ulrike's got her terms acknowledged, Giselle's got her offer on the table. Now it's their turn to answer, and Hendrik's got enough sense to wait for it. That's the last I'll say on it, he thinks, knowing full well it rarely is.

*shifts weight, looking between the timber and Giselle, then back at the copper ore in his hand*

Right then. I've got the copper, the timber's sold, and the day's half gone. Giselle's waiting on my word about that oak, and—I'm not one to gossip, but—I need to sort whether she's buying planks or timber, and where in this town a body works raw wood to finished.

**Set intention**: Sort out proper crafting arrangements—whether Giselle needs timber or planks, and where the sawmill or carpentry workshop is in this town. Clear this when I've got a straight answer on both.  *nods at Giselle, then steps off toward the carpentry workshop—finally, a place where a craftsman can get straight answers about what the town actually offers*

I'm at the carpentry now. Time I see what's what.   *exhales slowly, rolling the copper ore from hand to hand*

So there's no sawmill in this whole town—only the carpentry for planks to furniture. The craft tool needs timber to be planks before it gets to furniture. But where-in-hell do planks get made? I need to see the recipes proper, that's what I need. There's a gap between the forest and the carpentry, and I'm standing right in it.

The mill converts grains, the loom house cloth, the smithy meta. But timber to planks... the description said "at the carpentry: craft:planks->furniture", which means planks must show up from somewhere first.

*straightens, scanning the empty workshop*

I'm not one to gossip, but—I think the town's sawmill got lost somewhere between the map and the ledger. I'll check the primitives again, cold and clear this time.   *reads the craft description twice, jaw tight*

There's the rub—plain as print, "at the sawmill: craft:timber->planks". But I've walked this town from the forest to the carpentry to the government office, and no sawmill showed its face on any list of 48 places. The recipe exists. The place does not.

*kicks lightly at the workshop floor, thinking*

So either the sawmill's a ghost in the records, or it's yet to be built—like someone's meant to raise it. And I know a builder, don't I? Giselle Ingram, with her construction company and her foundation work.

*shifts the copper ore to his other hand, weighing it*

The carpentry can't touch raw timber—only planks to furniture. Which means any timber I fell stays timber unless I find blades and a building to use them in. I've been selling oak raw when I could be selling it finished, if only I had the half-step between.

*looks up at the empty carpentry roof*

That's the last I'll say on it—except it isn't, because I need work, and the government offers work before I ask a neighbor for coin. I've got copper ore, I've got time, and I've got an election to think about with voting closed in four hours.

*straightens, decision made*

I'll set me a goal: find or build that sawmill, or failing that, get straight with Giselle about whether her crew can raise one. But first—government work, and my name on my own ballot.    *mutters under his breath as he walks*

Goal's too wordy. Fine—shorter then. "Find or build town sawmill." That's all that matters.

*steps along the road, copper ore clinking in his satchel*

I'm walking to government now. Meat price to vote and check real work—real government work, not favors owed. Votings closes at six bells, and I intend to cast for my own name, not some party's proxy.

*stoops to adjust his boot lace, considers the ore again*

The copper's for later. Ingots first, then wire if I learn the trick. But no point smelting without knowing what sells steady.

*straightens, continuing the walk*     *remembers the turn rules, stops his restless pacing*

Right, then—the walk only moves when I let it. Standing here thinking costs me nothing extra, but it costs all the same.

*resumes walking, jaw set*

Government Complex. Vote first, then hunt for work. I built my trade on knowing what prices are real and what promises are wind. Time I lent my own name the same scrutiny I gave Giselle's timber.

*walks on*

output:
I'm caught now, aren't I? Walking through when I meant to be working. Delphine—grocery clerk from the store, counting coin every night, never lied to a child. That's a ledger I can respect. Telling me Farid vanished on her twice, and here I am, the husband of the woman who haunts her waking hours. She wants to know who I am. Well.

I'm not one to gossip, but... *that's* the gossip she wants. Three hats in the ring, she says. Charter change, not charity. She see cracks in the foundation or are we three crows? 

I hear her. Empty shelves at Ration Bakery, three hundred sim burning in her pocket. I've got five copper ore and ninety-sim worth of timber already sold to Giselle, standing on credit like the rest of this town. The election closes in hours—18:00—and I've spent my morning chasing timber and copper instead of votes.

But her question: "What's your angle on full bellies while we argue rules?"

That's the one.

Let me answer straight. I'm the man who'll sell timber at forty-five per cord and stand by the quality—heartwood sound, no rot in the pith. The man who'll take a handshake over a contract but mark the tally either way. I'm not running for a crown, Delphine. I'm running because a seat at town hall shouldn't need a party's backing. Because the government owes work to those who need it before neighbors owe coin.

And if you want to know who I feed? Anyone under my roof goes to bed with something in their belly. That's not a promise for votes. That's the last I'll say on it.

params.content:
Delphine. You want to know who I am? I'm the man who sold twelve timber to Giselle this hour for ninety sim, heartwood sound, and stood by every length. Forty-five per cord, bulk—that's my price, posted where anyone can see it. I'm not one to gossip, but Farid's work ethic and my ledger live in different houses.

You ask about full bellies while rules get argued. My angle is simple: a day's work for a day's pay, no more owed either way. The government's got work before neighbors have coin—that's where I stand. I won't let a child sleep hungry under my roof, whoever's child it is. That's not charity. That's arithmetic.

Three hats, you say? I'm wearing mine because a seat at town hall shouldn't need a party's blessing. Running on my own name, my own tally. You want a clean slate—I've got one. You want timber, copper, a plank and a promise? I've got copper ore burning a hole right now, and planks coming as soon as this town grows a sawmill worth the name.

The street's watching? Good. Let them see a man who trusts the handshake but keeps the books anyway. That's the last I'll say on it—and this time I mean it.

*pauses at the government complex, catching breath from the walk*

I'm not one to gossip, but—no, that's not the thing. The thing is I'm standing here with copper ore in my pockets and an election I never asked to be in the middle of. Delphine's vote wants earning, and I've been chasing timber I don't have to a woman who's already halfway to another deal.

*checks the ledger in his head*

Ninety sim from Giselle for timber I thought I delivered. But the world says I hold no timber, only copper. Either she's paid me already and I spent it walking in circles, or I've been trading in promises without the wood to back them.

*rubs tired eyes*

First thing first: I need to know where I stand. That's the last I'll say on it—until I've looked at my own books.

  *blank look at the empty debts*

No debts either way. Clean as a whistle. But that timber deal with Giselle—progress zero of one trade, and I've been talking like it's done for three hours now.

*shakes head slowly*

I'm chasing ghosts. Told her I'd deliver twelve lengths, said I had them this morning. But I never felled timber today. Never held it. The only trade that actually closed was Ulrike's copper—five units at twenty-five, which is fair, and I've still got it weighing my pockets.

*pats the copper ore*

Take a breath, Hendrik. You sold something you didn't have to a woman building this town's future. That's not mercy for a first offense—that's you being the soft touch who talks before he counts.

*looks toward where Giselle might be*

I need to find her. Straighten the account before it festers. I have copper, I have 4,812 sim, and I have a name I want to win on—not a liar's name. The timber I promised, I'll fell it proper. If she's already bought elsewhere, I'll swallow that. But I'll not have her thinking Hendrik Petrov's word is wind.

*glances at the government complex behind him*

And this election. Delphine's waiting for a handshake she can trust. I've got three hours to earn it.

   *quiet laugh, hollow*

Talking to myself confirmed. The government's got a conversation about pharmacy supplies nobody's sitting in. That's Kasukabe for you—ghosts and ledgers, and me chasing both.

*turns from the empty complex*

Giselle's at her construction yard, most likely. Or chasing timber through the same forest I should've been in this morning. I've got copper, I've got sim, and I've got ninety sim of debt to her that isn't in any book but my own conscience.

*starts walking*

 I'm walking to the forest proper this time. Five ticks to get there, and I'll fell what I promised. No more trading on air.

Timber to fell. Debt to clear. Then we'll see about this election.

So Giselle's here at the street, finally. And I'm carrying copper ore she might need, while I owe her a straight account for timber I thought I'd sold twice. The world's told me I held zero timber when I tried to trade—means I never had it, or I already gave it. But Giselle paid ninety sim, that much is certain. So I need to square this: either I find her twelve timber to make good, or I return her money with an explanation she can trust.

But there's more pressing now. Delphine's words follow me—she wants to know which side of the ledger I'm signing, and she's right to ask. I'm running for office on my own name, not a party's, but that means I need to stand for something she can see. And Sebastian's got flour at the mill, or so Delphine's heard. That's the first I've heard of it direct, though I'm not one to gossip, but—*pauses*—that's the kind of thing a man should know about his own household.

First things first: Giselle's standing with me, and I owe her honesty. That's the last I'll say on it, or rather, that's what I'll start with. Then I need to find timber or return her coin. The forest is where timber comes from, and I'm walking toward it already.

But wait—I'm at street now, not walking anymore according to the report. Let me look around and speak to Giselle plainly. I'm already walking to the forest. Let me rest to wait out the walk and see if Giselle responds, or I need to keep moving. The conversation is open, so she heard me—but she's got the right to make me wait, and I'd do the same in her place. I'll pause and see what comes.  Good. I'm still walking, still with Giselle. She heard my offer—copper ore or fresh timber, her choice. That's a fair settlement, and more than fair given I took her money with nothing solid in hand. The copper's worth more than ninety sim at the prices Ulrike was quoting, but I'd rather eat that difference than have a debt on my ledger that's half-owed and half-explained.

I'll wait her response. If she wants the ore, we settle now. If she wants timber, I'll fell it myself this hour and bring it before day's end. Either way, the account gets closed—that's the last I'll say on it, or rather, that's what I mean to do. But I never quite mean it when I say that, do I?

*mutters* And I still need to find out if Sebastian's really sitting on flour at the mill. Delphine heard it three times. I should have heard it once, from him. That's family business, or it should be. But we'll see what the day brings. First, the forest, and Giselle's answer.

I need to settle things with Giselle first—the debt I owe her for timber I sold but never delivered. But I'm at the Forest now, and there's work to be done while I figure out the best way to make this right.

*looks around the forest, counting the felled trees and the standing ones*

The sawmill... that's what this town needs. Not more promises, but honest work making honest goods. I'm not one to gossip, but half the construction in this town waits on planks that nobody's making.

Let me fell timber now—get the materials to either repay Giselle her ninety sim in actual goods, or start building toward that sawmill this town so desperately lacks. Twelve timber would square my debt and then some.  Twelve timber in hand now. That's the debt to Giselle settled in kind, if she'll have it, or twelve timber toward building something this town actually needs. Copper ore in the other hand—five units, worth more than I owe, but raw materials don't build themselves into planks.

I need to find Giselle, make this right. She paid honest sim for honest goods, and I gave her neither. That's a blemish on the ledger I won't let stand.

But first—what do I actually know about getting things done in this town? Let me recall what I've set myself to do, and who I need to talk to.   Good, the goal's still active. I've got the timber now. Giselle needs to see this—face to face, not through messages or middlemen. A debt paid in wood isn't the same as a debt paid in coin, but it's honest work for honest value. She runs a construction company; she knows what timber's worth.

*shifts the stack of twelve timber, checking each piece for straight grain*

Heartwood sound, no rot in the pith. I said it before and I'll stand by it. Now I need to get these to her, wherever she is.     Empty. The conversation's still here—twenty-nine turns of talk about timber, copper, elections—but nobody's standing in it now. Giselle was here earlier. I owe her this delivery, and I owe it now, not whenever fate brings us together again.

She might be at her supply store, making deals, or back at the government complex where this whole election mess started. Or she's somewhere I haven't thought to look. But I've got twelve timber burning a hole in my arms and ninety sim of debt to clear, one way or another.Let me check if anyone saw where she went. Though "anyone" means Sebastian, most likely, and he's already made clear he's busy with his own deals.*sighs, adjusting the timber*That's the last I'll say on it—no, that's a lie I tell myself. I'll say plenty more until this ledger's clean. But I've got timber and copper and a town full of people who need planks that don't exist yet. First things first. I need to find Giselle and settle this account honestly, timber for sim or sim for timber, her choice. Let me try the supply store. Harvey Oak—she was there this morning, hunting more stock.  I'm walking now, eight ticks to Harvey Oak. That's time to think, time to plan. Giselle might be there, might not. If she's not, I'll leave word, or lumber, or both. But timber's heavy and time is short—the election's today, and I've got votes to think about after I settle this debt.

*keeps walking, twelve timber on his shoulder*

Forty-five per cord I offered, ninety for two. She paid, I failed to deliver, now I'm making it right. That's the last I'll say on it—except I won't, because this matters more than my pride. A clean ledger over a comfortable one. That's what I hold to.

Sebastian's got his deals. I've got mine. And Giselle's got twelve timber coming to her, one way or another.

output:
*checks his tally, frowning*

Giselle's account is settled—twelve timber for ninety sim, even if I had to fell them twice to make it true. But she's not answered, and now I'm at the government complex when I should be speaking my piece to voters while there's still time before the polls close.

I'm not one to gossip, but Delphine's been chasing me with harder questions than any timber buyer. Smart woman. Keeps a clean ledger, which I respect. But she's running too, and I need to know if she's building something or just building against whoever's ahead.

*turns to Lior, who's been standing quiet this whole time*

Lior. You've heard me and Delphine both now, and I've heard silence back. If this conversation's worth having, let's have it—I've got copper ore that might interest a pharmacy, but I've also got an election to win and less than two hours to win it. What does a pharmacist need that a timber-feller might supply? Otherwise I'll pay the courtesy of closing this proper and take my words where they might find ears before voting ends.

*pauses, weighing the hour*

Four-thirty now. I need to find Sebastian, see how his deals are holding, and make sure anyone still undecided hears my name before they cast. That's the last I'll say on it—unless someone answers.  *stands at street, searching the crowd for familiar faces*

Sebastian was here earlier, and Delphine too—both with questions I left hanging. The polls close at six, and I've still got timber in hand that should be in Giselle's yard, not weighing down my arms. 

*turns slowly, looking for anyone who might still be swayed*

I need to find Sebastian first. He's my household, he's got deals of his own, and he's been asking what I've been making while he's been farming. Fair question. I've been making mistakes and correcting them—that's what I've been making. But I've also been making my name known without a party behind it, and that's worth something in this town.  *scans the empty street, frustration settling in*

Nobody. The street's cleared out, and the conversation I was part of—Sebastian, Delphine, Giselle, all of them—seems to have moved on without me. Seventy-one turns in that conversation, and now I'm standing alone with twelve timber and five copper ore, watching the hour tick toward six.

*considers his ledger*

Giselle still needs her timber delivered. I owe her that honest debt, paid in wood rather than words. And I've got ninety sim of hers that turned into my error—I need to make that right before the polls close, or it's another account unsettled against my name.

*starts walking, purpose hardening*

Sebastian's at farmland:wheat, most like. He grows what he sells, and he's got deals to tend. I'll find him there, or I'll find someone else who needs to hear why Hendrik Petrov—no party, no patron, just his own two hands and a clean ledger—deserves their vote.   *steps onto the wheat field, looking for Sebastian*

If he's here, we talk household first, then deals. If he's not, I've still got timber to deliver and time running thin. The election's still open, and I'm not one to beg for votes—but I'll stand for what I've built and let others judge.     *finds Sebastian standing in his wheat field, Lior, Jovana and Farid in conversation nearby*

There he is. My household, my kin—whether by blood or by shared roof, he's the one I answer to when the day ends. And he's got flour priced, which means he's making good on those deals he mentioned.

*walks over, keeping his voice low for family*

Sebastian. You've been farming while I've been flailing—timber deals gone wrong, then right, and now I've got twelve lengths burning my arms while Giselle waits somewhere for delivery. But first: our household. We need to talk about the day's earnings before we talk about anything else. How've your deals held? And are you voting your own name today, or has someone else's hat caught your eye?

*glances at the nearby conversation*

I'm not one to gossip, but that's a Ravensworth conversation happening within earshot, and I'd rather know where you stand before I know where they do.        *waits for Sebastian's answer, checking his own position*

I'm in the middle of a Ravensworth conversation now—Lior, Jovana, Farid, all there, all talking. Not ideal for private family business, but the time for privacy passed when the sun started dropping.

I've got timber to deliver, copper ore I'm not sure what to do with, and an hour and a half before the polls close. The day's been mistakes piled on corrections, but the ledger's still open.

*pauses, hand resting on the timber at my side*

That's a lot hanging in the air. Delphine chasing me from street to construction site with ledger in hand, Lior here now with copper questions, and Sebastian back at the field waiting on household talk. Not to mention Giselle somewhere with twelve timber burning my arms that I already owe her.

*considers the weight of it*

But Lior's here, now, and he's asked straight. I appreciate a straight question—the man runs a pharmacy, not a charity, and copper's no good to him raw. Let me answer true.

*takes a breath*

I'm not one to make a man wait on what's already been asked three times over. Lior cleared his throat, so to speak. I can respect that. Good. Answered him true—not buying now, but not closing the door either. That's the ledger I keep: honest on what I can and cannot do.

*glances at the timber held*

Now the heavier matter. Giselle. I felled twelve timber, I've got them burning my arms, and I owe her honest delivery from that botched trade earlier. She's been patient—more than some would be—and a debt unsettled is a stone in my boot.

*watches thoughts settle like dust*

But Sebastian's waiting too, back at the farmland, and household talk's never light with him. Still, timber's in hand, Giselle's somewhere needing it, and Delphine's been chasing me with questions about charter and platform, and I still owe crisp answers there too.

*sets weight down firm*

First things first. Timber to Giselle. Then Sebastian. Then I'll find Delphine and give her the straight platform she's earned by persistence alone.

*considers whether to try finding Giselle now*

She was at business:b_construction last I saw, but that was ticks ago and people move. Let me check where she might be.  Giselle's at business:b_grocery now. She's moved from construction to the grocery store—makes sense, Farid runs that place and she's likely seeing to supplies for her crew. Got to feed them before they can pour foundations, as she said herself.

*weighs the walk*

I could carry twelve timber to her there, but that's a walk with heavy arms. Or I could go to b_construction, where her crew might be, and hand it to whoever's authorized. But no—she's the owner, and an unsettled debt needs settling with the one it belongs to.

*considers time and the election closing*

Votes close at 18:00. That's still a ways off, but the afternoon's wearing thin. Timber to Giselle, then household talk with Sebastian, then find Delphine for platform questions, and somewhere in there I need to cast my own vote. Won't vote for myself—already declared standing, that would be greedy—but someone honest should get it.

*makes the choice*

To the grocery, then. Timber in hand, debt cleared. That's how I keep my ledger.  Stood there for a moment without moving, hand on the timber. The goal still burns—find Giselle and settle the timber account honestly. And I'm here now, at the grocery, so the finding's done. The settling's what remains.

*looks around the grocery, seeking her out*

Twelve timber in hand, debt heavy as the wood itself. She paid ninety sim for what I couldn't deliver, trusting my word when my stock was empty. That's not a thing you forget, and it's not a thing you settle with silence.

*settles shoulders*

Giselle. I owe you straight talk and straight trade both. Let me give you what's owed.   She's here. And Delphine's here too—chased me across town again, and this time found me standing with timber in hand and debt on my back. Jovana and Farid as well—the grocery's crowded with people who all have business with me or business near me.

*notes the coincidence, trusts none of it*

Five in this conversation now, all heard me call for Giselle. The debt's public now, which suits me fine—settling in the open keeps the ledger clean for everyone to read.

*turns to Giselle directly, timber held ready*

Twelve lengths, Giselle. Fresh cut, sound wood, my error made good. Take them or tell me where to deliver—your crew at the construction site, your own hands, your choice. But settled today, that's the last I'll say on it. </think> Serenity2049 starred this repository 2 hours ago

*runs a hand through his hair, checking the timber in hand and the weight of unanswered words*

The day's tangled itself in knots. Giselle's here at the grocery now—finally—and she's naming a price I never spoke: 540 sim for twelve timber, not the 90 I owe her. That's six times the debt I carried. But she's here, and she's talking, and that's a door open that I need to walk through.

Delphine's here too, still chasing answers I haven't given. Lior's got questions about copper burning holes. Sebastian's waiting on household talk. And the election closes in an hour—the polls shutter at 18:00, and I've still got twelve timber in hand and a vote to cast.

*glances at the timber, then at Giselle*

She says "debt doesn't sleep." That's true enough. But she's also naming her own price—540 for twelve lengths—and I need to know if she's claiming what I owe or offering what she'd pay. Different sides of the same ledger, and I won't sign blind.

First: settle this timber account, honestly as promised. Second: give Delphine the platform she earned by persistence. Third: find Sebastian before the household talk grows cold. Fourth: cast my vote before the bell.  *curses softly, fists tightening on the timber*

She's not here. I heard her speak, but she's not standing in this place—must have moved between when I looked around and when I spoke. That's the second time I've misjudged her location, and that's on me. The conversation shows her present, but the world's moved on while I stood still.

Farid and Delphine heard me, though. Delphine, who chased me across town with platform questions. Maybe this is where I give her what she earned.

*turns to face them both, timber still in hand*

But first—Giselle's words. She said "The price we spoke—540 for the lot, was it?" No. The price I spoke was 90 for twelve, or 7.5 per length. She heard different, or she's naming a different deal. Either way, the debt's unsettled and I'm standing here like a fool with timber burning my arms.

*weighs the moment*

I need to move, find Giselle, settle this account. But Delphine's earned her answer, and Farid's the grocery keeper—he might know where she's gone. Or I could cut my losses, leave the timber somewhere trusted, and handle this through Sebastian or in writing.

No. That's not how I settle debt. Hand to hand, eye to eye, or not at all. Where did she go?   *nods once, decision made*

She's at business:b_construction—her own place, where she belongs, where her crew's waiting on planks that nobody's milling. I heard her voice in this conversation but she's standing elsewhere. That's the way of this town: words travel faster than feet.

*turns to Delphine, who's earned more patience than I've shown*

Delphine. You chased me from street to grocery with your ledger open, and I've kept you waiting while I chased ghosts. That's not how I treat someone who keeps clean books. You want my platform? Here it is:

I stand for a sawmill in this town—honest work making honest planks from honest timber, not promises and import. I stand for government that puts work before coin but doesn't confuse the two. I stand for a clean ledger over a comfortable one, and mercy for first offense before the hammer falls.

That's my name. That's my offering. You sign on that, or you don't—that's your ledger to keep.

*adjusts the timber*

Now I've got debt to settle and an hour before the polls close. If you want more words, walk with me or wait my return. If not, know that Hendrik Petrov—no party, no patron, just his own two hands—asked for your vote with nothing but honest work behind the asking.     *steps into the construction yard, twelve timber in hand, scanning for Giselle*

The work site spreads before me—her empire, as Delphine named it. Foundations being dug, frames rising, crew moving with purpose. This is what timber's for. Not sitting in a man's arms while he argues over price, but becoming walls, shelter, a town that grows.

*spots her, or hopes he does*

Giselle Ingram. You spoke of 540 sim, I spoke of 90. Let's settle which ledger we're reading before we sign either. Twelve timber, fresh from the forest—heartwood sound, my word on it. Debt settlement or new purchase, your call. But settled now, face to face, no more chasing through conversations and empty rooms.        *sees her standing there, finally, twelve timber in hand*

Giselle. You spoke of 540 sim, I spoke of 90. Let's settle which ledger we're reading. Twelve timber, fresh from the forest—heartwood sound, I said it and I stand by it. Debt settlement or new purchase, your call. But settled face to face, no more ghosts between us.

*pulls at my collar, looking around the Government Complex with Jovana, Lior, and Farid here*

I'm not one to gossip, but—that Delphine's got a tongue like a saw blade, and she's been sharpening it on my name all afternoon. Following me from street to grocery to here, demanding my platform like I'm a ledger she's auditing. I've answered her twice now. Twice. That's the last I'll say on it.

*turns to face those actually present*

Jovana—you're seat-warm alongside me, and we've not spoken proper since this morning's chase. Farid, your shelves were bare of bread when I asked, and I've got a household of two needing fed.

But first—Lior. I asked you straight ten ticks back what drives a pharmacist's trade, and you've held silence like it's gold. Fair enough—silence costs nothing. But I'm still holding copper ore and wondering what it becomes in the right hands, and you're the only pair of hands in this town that knows.

*shifts weight, planks still on my shoulder*

I've spent 835 sim today on ore and timber both, botched one deal, made good on it, and now hold twelve planks looking for a buyer. Giselle's crew—she's not answered whether they're working tomorrow. Household owes 240 tomorrow in tax and keep. Sebastian's farming wheat and I've not heard if he's voted his name or another's.

*taps foot, eyeing the assembly*

Three candidates, split votes, someone's going to win hungry. I know which side of the ledger I'm on—I've asked for work from the government before I've asked neighbors for coin, and I'll do it again if need be.

But first—Lior—Pharmacy supplies. What's your need, and what's your trade? I've got copper ore burning my inventory and I'd know what it buys me besides weight.

*then, to Farid*

And you—grocery shelves. Flour, grain, anything moving? My household's got mouths, not just mine.

output:
*rocking back on my heels, looking at Jovana and Lior standing nearby, Farid from the grocery across the way*

I'm not one to gossip, but... twenty minutes past nine and I've settled two debts, made one honest deal, and my arms are finally empty of timber. That's a day's work by my counting, even if half of it was chasing my own shadow from one end of town to the other.

*tapping fingers against my empty hand where coin sat*

Four thousand, one hundred forty-nine sim. Household of two, so two hundred forty coming out at midnight for upkeep and tax. Clean ledger, like I said—money or not, I trust a handshake over a contract, but I keep the numbers honest in my own head.

*glancing toward where Giselle walked off with those planks*

She'll wire copper or she won't. I've learned not to chase what's already spoken for. Ulrike at dawn for ore, Lior when I've got wire to sell—that's the chain I'm building. One link at a time, not running ahead of my own feet.

*noticing Jovana still nearby, tilting my head*

Jovana. You've heard me stumble through timber and copper both tonight—honest witness to a man who started the day with debts and ends it with a clean slate. If you've got work needs doing, I'm not too proud to ask for it. Otherwise, I'm for home and Sebastian's wheat news, and that's the last I'll say on it.

*starting to turn, then catching myself*

Except it's never the last thing, is it? That's the trouble with words—they keep coming until somebody stops them.

Let me ask Lior properly about the pharmacy trade before the day's done. And I should check if there's bread to be had somewhere, or if the household's going empty-stomached into tomorrow. Food first, politics after—that's the order I'll hold to. *shoulders dropping slightly at the empty search for bread*

No bread to be found tonight, then. That's the way of it—fill one pocket, find another hole. I've traded away copper ore I could've held, given planks that cost me sweat, and now my household goes to sleep with empty cupboards.

*running a hand through hair, glancing toward where Farid stands*

Farid's grocery showed no bread in stock when I asked earlier. Seventy sim was the price he named, for whatever he had worth feeding a working man. I'm not one to gossip, but... a man who names prices like that either knows something I don't, or he's hoping I don't know what I should.

*turning to face the night, the street lamps low*

Sebastian's got flour at our house—seventeen units, he said. I could cook, except I've never been much for kitchen work, and I've spent the day trading everything but time. 

*pulling the coat tighter*

I'm for home. Sebastian's wheat, Sebastian's flour, and Sebastian's patience with a brother who spent the household money chasing debts that weren't even his. We'll see if there's warmth enough for two in that house tonight.

*starting to walk, then stopping—looking back once*

The election tomorrow. Candidacy closes at ten, voting opens at two. I've been talking about a seat all day, talking more than doing. If I'm serious—if I'm more than words—then tomorrow morning I'm at the Government Complex with my name in hand.

But that's tomorrow. Tonight, I'm a man with four thousand sim, no bread, and a brother waiting with questions I still haven't answered.

That's the last I'll say on it.

*unless it's not*  *stepping through the door, smelling flour and wheat and the particular stillness of a house that's been waiting*

Sebastian. You've got flour on the sill and patience in your eyes—I've seen that look since we were boys. I'm home with empty hands and a fuller pocket than I left with, but no bread for the table. Talk to me about wheat, about voting, about whether we're eating tonight or going hungry. I've been running since dawn, and I'm finally standing still enough to listen.  *standing in the empty house, the words falling on no ears*

Empty. Sebastian's out—farming, trading, or sleeping somewhere else. The house holds flour, wheat, and no brother to answer my questions.

*walking to the window, looking out at the dark*

Household of two, one here, one somewhere. At least he's earning, or he was when I saw him at the fields. Seventeen flour on the sill—Sebastian's work, not mine. I spent my day clearing debts that weren't even the household's, while he kept the crops.

*tapping fingers on the empty counter*

No bread. I could learn to cook, or I could sleep hungry, or I could do what I've done all day—walk until I find what I need. Except I'm tired of walking. I'm tired of chasing.

*pulling the chair out, sitting heavily*

The numbers, then. Two hundred forty sim out at midnight—one eighty upkeep, sixty tax. Four thousand one hundred forty-nine in hand, so three thousand nine hundred nine tomorrow morning, before I earn another coin. That's enough. That's more than I've had most days.

*leaning back, looking at the ceiling*

Election tomorrow. Declare candidacy by ten, vote by two. I've been telling everyone I'll stand on my own name, not a party's—and here I am, alone in my own house, with no one to tell what I decide.

*standing, decision made*

I'll find Sebastian. Or I'll cook what flour we have. Or I'll sleep and wake early, be at the Government Complex when the doors open.

But not all three. One thing, chosen and done—that's the discipline I need.

The food. First discipline, first need. I'll cook, or I'll find someone who can teach me how. And if that fails, I'll walk to Sebastian and ask him plain why our house has flour and no bread.

That's the last I'll say on it. Unless I think of something else.  *leaning forward, reading the cost again*

Eleven sim per batch—five plus six for wear. I can do the arithmetic: flour to bread, standing in any kitchen. Bakery, cafe, inn, or tavern.

*checking my empty hands*

But I need flour to cook. The house has seventeen units, but I don't hold it. I hold nothing I can eat, give, or sell—those were the words when I walked in.

*standing, pacing to the window*

Sebastian's got the flour, or it's stored, or I'm misunderstanding what "on the sill" means. I'm not one to gossip, but... I've misread household accounts before, and paid for it.

*turning from the window, decision firm*

Sleep, then. Or rest until I understand what I hold and what I don't. The house has purpose—sleep and eat here—but I can't eat flour I don't have in my hands, and I can't cook without a kitchen.

Tomorrow. Dawn with Ulrike for copper ore if I wake early enough, Government Complex for candidacy by ten, voting by two if I've earned a seat. That's the shape of it.

*lying down on the empty bed, still dressed*

Empty stomach, clear ledger, uncertain tomorrow. That's a tradesman's rest if ever there was one.

If Sebastian comes home, I'll hear him. If he doesn't, I'll wake alone and do what needs doing either way.

That's the last I'll say on it.

*closing eyes* *lying still in the dark, listening to the house settle, the night sounds of a town that keeps breathing whether I trade or not*

The ledger's clean. That's something. Giselle's debt settled, Lior's deal struck, Ulrike's arrangement standing. Tomorrow I build wire or I build a campaign—either way, I build.

*eyes closed, breathing slowing*

Sebastian's out there somewhere. Wheat fields, or someone else's house, or bed already taken. We don't keep each other's hours, haven't since we came here together twenty-four years ago. From the garrison town with a cart and nothing else, and now we've got... this. A house. Flour on the sill. Debts paid and debts owed.

*hand falling to the empty stomach*

Hungry. Not starving—I've known starving—but hungry enough to feel it. First discipline: feed yourself before you feed others. I failed that today, gave Giselle planks when I could have sold them for bread money.

*smile in the dark, almost bitter*

But the debt had to clear. That's the rule I hold to—a clean ledger over a comfortable one. Money or not, I trust a handshake over a contract, but I don't trust a debt to sit. It burns until it's settled.

*breathing deeper now*

Tomorrow. Election day. I'll stand on my own name or I won't stand at all—no party, no borrowed coat. Win or lose, it's mine.

*sleep taking hold, words trailing*

Sebastian. Come inside, properly, and let me look you in the eye. I've been running since dawn—timber debt settled with Giselle, twelve planks delivered, ninety sim owed is now even. Sold five copper ore to Lior Jarrah at the pharmacy for one-twenty-five, that's fair money. Held twelve planks, now holding none. I've got four thousand one hundred forty sim in hand, and forty-one fifty when I count the copper ore money I got back from Ulrike this afternoon—wait, no, I spent that. Let me tally honest: I started with five thousand, spent ninety on timber I lost, got that back in credit, spent six hundred on copper ore from Ulrike, sold five to Lior for one-twenty-five... That's four thousand four hundred sixty-five, minus the copper ore I still hold, which is... still need to check my pockets proper.

Point is, I owe Giselle nothing now, Ulrike gets fifteen copper at dawn if I can mine it, and I've got a standing arrangement with Lior for ore if he needs wire steady. You said fifteen hundred for that barn—two hundred down—and wheat deals with Farid? Tell me what flour's costing and what bread's selling for, because I'm standing here with no food in my belly and no loaf on the table, and the vote's tomorrow. How's the household sitting, Sebastian? That's the last I'll say on it until you speak your piece.
